result.topic_en: Euler gives a second integration of the differential equation by introducing q = x − y, obtaining √X − √Y = √(Δ + Cqq), shows this agrees with the earlier algebraic integral, and begins the case where the sum dx/√X + dy/√Y vanishes.
result.transcription:
) 34 (

§. 31. Alio vero inſuper modo eandem aequatio-
nem differentialem propoſitam integrare poterimus, intro-
ducendo literam $q = x - y$; tum enim habebimus
$\frac{2\,ddq}{dt} = X' - Y'$. At vero erit
$X' - X' = 2\,C\,q + 3\,D\,q\,(x+y)$
vbi iterum patet ſtatui debere tam $D = 0$ quam $E = 0$,
vt integratio, multiplicando per $dq$, ſuccedat. Hoc autem
notato erit integrale $\frac{dq^2}{dt^2} = \text{Conſt} + C\,q\,q$, ideoque
$\frac{dq}{dt} = \sqrt{(\Delta + C\,q\,q)}$.

§. 32. Cum igitur ſit $\frac{dq}{dt} = \sqrt{X} - \sqrt{Y}$, hoc
integrale ita erit expreſſum:
$\sqrt{X} - \sqrt{Y} = \sqrt{(\Delta + C\,q\,q)}$
quae aequatio ſumtis quadratis abit in hanc:
$2\,A + B\,(x+y) + C\,(x\,x + y\,y) - 2\sqrt{X\,Y}$
$= \Delta + C\,(x-y)^2$ ſiue
$2\,A + B\,(x+y) + 2\,C\,x\,y - 2\sqrt{X\,Y} = \Delta$
vnde fit
$2\sqrt{X\,Y} = 2\,A - \Delta + B\,(x+y) + 2\,C\,x\,y$,
vbi ſi ponatur $2\,A - \Delta = -F$ aequatio ab ante in-
venta prorſus non diſcrepat.

§. 33. Quod ſi autem propoſita fuiſſet aequatio
$\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(A + B\,x + C\,x\,x)}}$ [?] $+ \frac{dy}{\sqrt{(A + B\,y + C\,y\,y)}} = 0$,
integralia ante inuenta ad hunc caſum referentur, ſi mo-
do loco $\sqrt{Y}$ ſcribatur $-\sqrt{Y}$; vnde patet pro hoc caſu
haberi hanc aequationem:
$\sqrt{X} - \sqrt{Y} = \sqrt{(\Delta + 2\,B\,(x+y) + C\,(x+y)^2)}$

items.english: where again it is evident that one must set both D = 0 and E = 0 for the integration, by multiplying by dq, to succeed.

items.english: where, if one sets 2A − Δ = −F, the equation does not differ at all from the one found before.
